name: Rainforest (Lowland Rainforest)
summary: Nigeria's cocoa and oil-palm heartland across the humid south-west, south-east and south-south.
description: Humid lowland rainforest on the southern coastal plain: tall, multi-storey evergreen forest on deeply leached, acidic soils. The wet season is long with no real dry month. This is the historic and current cocoa, oil-palm, rubber and timber zone. Belt boundaries are approximate — the rainforest grades into derived savanna through a wide transition.
rainfall: 1,500–2,500 mm/yr (coastal forest zone >1,600 mm; FAO FOSA)
agriculture: Deep, leached ferralitic soils under high rainfall. Tree-crop agroforestry (cocoa, oil palm, kola) dominates, with root crops, plantain and vegetables in the understorey and on cleared ground.
economy: Cocoa, oil palm, rubber and timber — Nigeria's historic and current export tree-crop zone.

name: Derived Savanna
summary: The forest–savanna transition, farmed intensively for yam, cassava and maize.
description: Derived savanna is the transition mosaic between lowland rainforest and Guinea savanna: secondary forest, tall grasses and heavy farmland, produced by centuries of clearing and continuous cultivation. It carries some of Nigeria's densest rural populations. Belt boundaries are approximate.
agriculture: A mix of leached forest soils and savanna luvisols. Short fallows and dense population drive near-continuous cultivation of root crops and cereals.
economy: Yam, cassava, soybean and food grains feeding southern and Middle Belt markets.

name: Southern Guinea Savanna
summary: The southern half of the Guinea savanna — yam, shea and grain country.
description: Wooded savanna of the southern Middle Belt with parkland trees (shea, Daniellia, Isoberlinia), tall grasses and gallery forest along streams. It carries the deep ferric luvisols that support Nigeria's yam belt. Belt boundaries are approximate.
agriculture: Deep ferric luvisols support root crops and cereals; shea parklands are retained on farm fields across the belt and short fallow rotations are common.
economy: Yam, shea butter, grains and livestock corridors.

name: Northern Guinea Savanna
summary: The northern half of the Guinea savanna — sorghum, cowpea and cotton.
description: Drier Guinea savanna with open Isoberlinia–Daniellia woodland and shorter grass. This is the core grain-and-legume zone of northern Nigeria, with a longer dry season and dry-season fadama irrigation. Belt boundaries are approximate.
agriculture: Sandy-loam luvisols farmed with organic manure and short fallows, plus dry-season fadama irrigation along the inland valleys.
economy: Grains, legumes and cotton, with expanding dry-season irrigation.

name: Sudan Savanna
summary: Open-tree savanna of the far-north fringe — drier than Guinea, main cereal and legume zone.
description: Sudan savanna is Nigeria's northern crop-and-livestock belt with 500–900 mm annual rainfall, a shorter wet season (3–5 months) and scattered acacia and baobab trees. It covers most of Kano, Katsina, southern Sokoto, southern Borno, Jigawa, Bauchi and Gombe. Belt boundaries are approximate.
agriculture: Shallow sandy-loam soils with low organic matter — rely on organic manure, mulch and small-scale irrigation (fadamas). Wind erosion and desertification pressure the northern fringe.
economy: Cereals, legumes, livestock, irrigation dams and dry-season onion belts.

name: Sahel Savanna
type: Semi-arid vegetation belt at the desert fringe
summary: Semi-arid grass and acacia steppe on the northern desert boundary — pastoral and resilient dry-crop zone.
description: The Sahel is the narrow northernmost vegetation zone along the Niger border with under 500 mm annual rainfall and frequent droughts. It is dominated by short grass, sparse acacia and a pastoral economy of cattle, sheep and goats, with Lake Chad and the Komadugu–Yobe basins sustaining irrigation oases. Belt boundaries are approximate.
crops: Dryland rice (on fadamas where water is available)
agriculture: Very fragile sandy soils with low water-holding capacity — depend on drought-tolerant crops, water-harvesting structures and lake/fadama irrigation. Desertification and wind erosion are active challenges.
economy: Pastoralism, drought-millet, lake-basin irrigation and gum-arabic agroforestry.

name: Mangrove & Coastal Swamp
summary: The saltwater and swamp fringe of the coast, including the Lagos–Badagry coconut belt.
description: Tidal mangrove and brackish-to-freshwater swamp along the lagoon and delta fringe, with barrier beaches and estuaries. Salt-tolerant Rhizophora and Avicennia grow on waterlogged, saline mud. The belt includes the Lagos–Badagry coconut coast. Belt boundaries are approximate.
rainfall: >2,500 mm/yr in the delta and eastern coast; >1,600 mm across the forest zone (FAO FOSA)
agriculture: Saline, poorly aerated muds limit cultivation to stabilised, non-saline swamp and levee ridges; artisanal fisheries are economically vital.
economy: Coconut, oil palm, swamp rice and coastal fisheries.

name: Niger Delta
summary: Africa's largest wetland delta where the Niger meets the Atlantic — Nigeria's petroleum heartland.
description: The delta covers roughly 70,000 km² of mangrove, freshwater swamp and barrier islands. It holds the bulk of Nigeria's oil and gas, a dense creek network, and highly politicised environmental and federal-revenue issues. Belt boundaries are approximate.
crops: Oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) — heart of the smallholder oil-palm belt
Plantain and banana — staple on levee soils
Cassava — garri, lafun and fufu processing
Yam — white and yellow yam in the drier northern fringe
Rice — lowland swamp and fadama paddies
Cocoyam — shade-tolerant tuber under palm canopy
Fluted pumpkin (ugu) — widely intercropped leaf vegetable
Vegetables: amaranth, okra, peppers, garden egg
Coconut palm — barrier beaches and island fringes
Mangrove (Rhizophora, Avicennia) — fuelwood, poles and fisheries habitat
Fish, shrimp and crab artisanal fisheries — Nigeria's richest coastal fishery
agriculture: Hydromorphic gleysols, peat and alluvial deposits on seasonally flooded flats, backswamps and levees. Oil-palm agroforest dominates the better-drained levee ridges; fisheries are economically vital.
economy: Oil and gas, fisheries, boat transport, refining and oil-palm agroforestry.

name: Montane / Plateau
summary: Nigeria's cool highlands — Irish potato, temperate vegetables and highland grains.
description: Cool highland plateau and montane grassland/forest rising above the surrounding savanna — chiefly the Jos Plateau and the Mambilla highlands. Cooler temperatures and high orographic rainfall allow temperate crops that cannot be grown on the surrounding plains. Belt boundaries are approximate and patchy — it is an island belt, not a continuous zone.
rainfall: 1,400–4,000 mm/yr on the highlands; 5–20°C (FAO montane/plateau climate)
agriculture: Volcanic and basement-complex soils on plateau surfaces; the cool climate supports temperate root and vegetable crops alongside highland cereals.
economy: Irish potato (Plateau supplies roughly 90% of national output), temperate vegetables and highland grains.

name: Oban Hills
summary: Cross River rainforest highlands linked to the Oban sector of Cross River National Park.
description: The Oban Hills lie in the Cross River–Cameroon biodiversity hotspot with lowland and montane rainforest, drill monkeys and rare forest elephants. The terrain is rugged and heavily forested, and the belt is a sub-state highland within Cross River's rainforest. Belt boundaries are approximate.
rainfall: High rainforest rainfall, >2,000 mm/yr (FAO forest zone)
crops: Cocoa (Theobroma cacao) — shaded agroforestry in the park buffer zone
Oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) — semi-wild stands and plantation palms
Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) — smallholder rubber on gentler slopes
Plantain and banana — staple food of Efik and Ejagham communities
Cocoyam, sweet potato and taro — under-storey root crops
Okra, pepper and amaranth — backyard vegetables
Kolanut (Cola nitida & acuminata) — ceremonial cash crop
Bush mango (Irvingia gabonensis) — ogbono soup seeds
Raffia palm (Raphia spp.) — palm wine, thatch and fibre
Timber (mahogany, obeche, iroko) — protected inside the national park
agriculture: Acrisols and ferralsols on steep slopes — highly leached but suitable for tree crops. Land-use pressure is intense outside the park boundary with shifting cultivation and cocoa farms.
economy: Ecotourism, conservation and limited hill farming.
